p0c01.subject: The OSS assessment school at Station S (Willard estate, Fairfax VA), where Henry Murray's staff graded spy candidates on an impossible construction task — build a 5-foot cube from poles and blocks with two "helpers," Kippy (passive, wanders off for a drink) and Buster (aggressive, criticizes everything), who were staff plants instructed to sabotage. No candidate in the entire program ever completed the structure. The structure was never the grade.
p0c01.org: US Office of Strategic Services, Assessment Staff (Station S / Station W)
p0c01.why_kernel: It is the founding case of the instrument the chapter describes: a task designed so the artifact cannot be produced, precisely so the only remaining signal is behavior under undefined, hostile, shifting conditions — which is literally "you are not being graded on the design, you are being graded on whether they'd hand you an ambiguous project (a drop behind enemy lines) on Monday," and it explains why the modern round uses a deliberately vague prompt and a "now 100x" push instead of a knowledge test. Delete it and the reader can only be told the kernel as an assertion; with it they can derive why the prompt is vague on purpose, why option-listing scores low (Buster exists to punish it), and why the interviewer steers rather than answers.
p0c01.struggle: The staff could never validate their own instrument. Overseas field appraisals of OSS operatives came back unreliable and contradictory, correlations with actual performance were modest at best, and the assessment staff said so in print in their own book — they had built the most elaborate judgment-under-ambiguity exam ever attempted and could not prove it predicted anything. That is still the honest position of the design interview.
p0c01.consequence: Roughly five thousand candidates run through Station S and Station W between December 1943 and the OSS's dissolution in 1945, at real wartime cost; the method was then lifted wholesale into AT&T's Management Progress Study (1956) and became the corporate assessment center industry, and from there the modern multi-hour tech loop with its simulation rounds. Every "design Instagram" round is a descendant of Kippy and Buster.
leads: OSS Assessment Staff, "Assessment of Men: Selection of Personnel for the Office of Strategic Services" (Rinehart, 1948) — the Construction Test, Kippy and Buster, and the staff's own chapter on validity failure
Murray, H.A. & MacKinnon, D.W., "Assessment of OSS personnel," Journal of Consulting Psychology 10(2), 1946
Lenzenweger, M.F. (2015), reanalysis of the original OSS candidate assessment data, Journal of Personality Assessment
Bray, D.W. & Grant, D.L., "The assessment center in the measurement of potential for business management," Psychological Monographs 80(17), 1966 — the corporate descendant

p0c02.subject: PayPal's 2000–2001 fraud crisis and the Igor system: losing over $10M a month against under $1M of revenue to Russian carding rings, Max Levchin's team found that a fully automated fraud model went stale the moment it shipped because the adversary re-read the rules and moved. The fix was not a better model but a tool that put a human analyst inside the loop — Igor, named after the fraudster it caught — with a hundred people reading its graphics for anomalies. Thiel incorporated Palantir on that pattern in 2003, and the forward-deployed engineer sitting next to the analyst is why Palantir's decomp round grades finding the problem instead of designing the system.
p0c02.why_kernel: The chapter has no kernel line in kernels.md; its working core is "each loop is a scale model of that company's hardest recurring on-the-job failure, so generic prep loses." This is the one event where that causal chain is fully traceable in public: a hazard (an adversary who redefines the problem faster than you can model it) produced a job (an engineer embedded beside the person who actually holds the question) which produced an exam (decomp: who looks at this, and what do they decide with it). Delete it and the four playbooks read as arbitrary corporate quirks to be memorized; with it the reader can derive any company's exam from its production hazard — and can predict Anthropic's cost/p99 axis and Google's NALSD arithmetic from the same rule. It also replaces the chapter's invented Priya scene with the actual origin of the round that ended it.
p0c02.struggle: Igor never closed the problem. Every model edge decayed as the ring adapted, so the humans could never be removed from the loop — and Palantir inherited that permanent human cost as a business model, shipping engineers with the software. A decade of trying to productize the forward-deployed engineer out of the margin is disclosed as a risk in its own 2020 S-1; the round that eats LeetCode champions exists because the company still cannot automate the part that finds the problem.
p0c02.consequence: Fraud losses exceeding $10M/month against under $1M/month revenue in 2000 — an existential burn rate that PayPal survived to IPO in 2002 and sell to eBay for $1.5B; the same pattern was capitalized as Palantir in 2003 and the FDSE headcount model it forced still shapes the company's gross margins and its hiring bar.
leads: Eric M. Jackson, "The PayPal Wars" (2004) — insider account of the fraud crisis and Igor
Jessica Livingston, "Founders at Work" (2007), Max Levchin interview — the deliberate decision to let fraud run in order to observe it, and why automation alone failed
MIT Technology Review, "Digital Cash Payoff" (December 2001) — contemporaneous reporting naming Igor and the 100-person fraud team
Palantir Technologies Form S-1, SEC, August 2020 — the forward-deployed engineer model and its stated economics

p1c01.subject: Bob Braden at USC/ISI publishes T/TCP (RFC 1644) to delete the TCP three-way handshake round trip; security researchers kill it, and the IETF formally buries it in 2011
p1c01.why_kernel: The chapter's 5-RTT ledger (DNS 1 + TCP 1 + TLS 2 + request 1) reads like accumulated sloppiness until you see the one documented attempt to bill a round trip out of existence: the handshake RTT is not ceremony, it is the only proof that the peer's source address is real, and T/TCP shows exactly which guarantee you forfeit when you skip it — which is why TCP Fast Open needs cookies and QUIC 0-RTT still carries a replay caveat.
p1c01.struggle: You cannot delete a round trip for free. T/TCP's accelerated open let an attacker spoof a source address and get data accepted and acted upon before any handshake completed; implementations in FreeBSD and SunOS shipped it disabled by default, and it was never widely deployed. The IETF moved RFC 1644 to Historic in 2011 without a replacement. The round trip stayed because it was load-bearing.
p1c01.consequence: Every HTTPS connection on earth kept paying the extra handshake RTT for roughly twenty more years. The idea only returned with TCP Fast Open (RFC 7413, 2014), whose own measurements put the saving at 4–41% of page load time, and with QUIC folding transport and TLS into one handshake (RFC 9000, 2021) — both re-inheriting the same replay problem T/TCP died of.
leads: RFC 1644, 'T/TCP -- TCP Extensions for Transactions Functional Specification', R. Braden, July 1994
Charles M. Hannum, 'Security Problems Associated with T/TCP', September 1996
RFC 6247, 'Moving the Undeployed TCP Extensions ... to Historic Status', L. Eggert, May 2011
Radhakrishnan, Cheng, Chu, Jain, Raghavan, 'TCP Fast Open', ACM CoNEXT 2011

p1c02.subject: Andrew Birrell and Bruce Nelson build RPC for Cedar on the Dorado at Xerox PARC and are forced to write the contract down: a unique call identifier minted by the caller, a duplicate-suppression table held by the callee, and the published finding that 'exactly once' is unattainable across a network, so the caller must be told the truth about which semantics it actually bought
p1c02.org: Xerox PARC, Computer Science Laboratory (Cedar / Grapevine)
p1c02.why_kernel: The chapter opens on a frozen spinner and a second tap and calls it a contract question. This is where that contract was first written as a specification rather than an etiquette: the retry is safe only if the callee can recognise it, the recogniser is a call identifier plus a table at the endpoint (never client-side politeness), and no timeout value anywhere makes a lost reply distinguishable from a lost call. From one 1984 paper the reader derives why PUT is idempotent by construction, why POST needs a key the *server* stores, why DELETE must succeed on an already-deleted resource, and — via Waldo's rebuttal — why you cannot version a call away under a caller you do not control.
p1c02.struggle: They shipped at-most-once and said so in print. The duplicate table is bounded and must be garbage-collected, so a retry that arrives after the entry expires executes a second time; a server crash orphans in-flight calls with no clean answer; and the whole abstraction's selling point — that a remote call looks like a local one — is the thing Waldo, Wyant, Wollrath and Kendall demolished ten years later as the reason a generation of distributed systems shipped broken.
p1c02.consequence: RPC became the default shape of distributed programming for forty years — Sun RPC and NFS (1984-85), DCE, CORBA, Java RMI, Thrift, gRPC — and every one inherited the same unresolved semantics, which is why the idempotency key is a product feature in every payments API written since. Stripe's Idempotency-Key header is Birrell and Nelson's call identifier with a billing address attached.
leads: A. D. Birrell & B. J. Nelson, 'Implementing Remote Procedure Calls', ACM TOCS 2(1), February 1984, pp. 39-59 (also Xerox CSL-83-7)
Bruce Jay Nelson, 'Remote Procedure Call', PhD thesis, Carnegie Mellon CMU-CS-81-119 / Xerox CSL-81-9, 1981 — the enumeration of call semantics (exactly-once, at-most-once, at-least-once)
Waldo, Wyant, Wollrath & Kendall, 'A Note on Distributed Computing', Sun Microsystems Laboratories TR-94-29, November 1994
RFC 1831 (ONC RPC) and the NFS duplicate request cache, for the same mechanism in a shipped protocol

p1c03.subject: Pat Selinger's team at IBM San Jose teaches System R to choose between a sequential scan and an index, and in doing so writes down the 'matching columns' rule
p1c03.why_kernel: Leftmost-prefix and 'a range predicate on a kills the use of b' look like arbitrary MySQL folklore until you read where they were defined. Selinger's paper counts, for a set of predicates, how many index columns they match — a prefix of the sort order, stopping at the first range — because an index key is a concatenation sorted lexicographically. Both rules in the kernel are corollaries of one 1979 costing definition, and the chapter's 'a low-cardinality index loses to a scan' is that cost model doing its job.
p1c03.struggle: The optimizer has to guess how many rows a predicate returns before running it. System R's model assumed uniform value distribution and statistical independence between predicates, and hardcoded 1/10 selectivity for anything it could not measure. Those assumptions were known to be wrong when written, are still in every mainstream optimizer, and are the origin of essentially every bad plan an engineer has ever debugged.
p1c03.consequence: System R's papers were published in the open while IBM sat on the product. Oracle read them and shipped a commercial SQL database first; IBM's SQL/DS and DB2 arrived years later. The paper's cost framework became the shared substrate of every relational optimizer since, meaning the whole industry inherited the 1979 uniformity assumption along with it.
leads: Selinger, Astrahan, Chamberlin, Lorie, Price, 'Access Path Selection in a Relational Database Management System', ACM SIGMOD 1979, pp. 23–34 (DOI 10.1145/582095.582099)
Astrahan et al., 'System R: Relational Approach to Database Management', ACM TODS 1(2), June 1976
'Pat Selinger Speaks Out', ACM SIGMOD Record oral-history interview (Marianne Winslett)

p1c04.subject: HealthCare.gov opens on 1 October 2013 sized for 50,000–60,000 concurrent users and takes 250,000, after a pre-launch test showed it breaking at about 1,100
p1c04.org: US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services / CGI Federal / QSSI
p1c04.why_kernel: This derives both halves of the kernel and its stated boundary. The number did pick the architecture — capacity was provisioned against a concurrency estimate — and the architecture was still wrong, because the divisor was an average day and launch day of a statutory national deadline has peak-to-average nothing like 2–5×. Delete this and '2–5× peak' reads as a safe default instead of a number that a correlated, calendar-driven burst blows through by an order of magnitude.
p1c04.struggle: The launch date was written in legislation and could not move. The load test that mattered ran days before go-live and showed the site failing at roughly 1,100 concurrent users, and CMS launched anyway without the required readiness verification. The requirement that users create an account before browsing plans — a policy decision made late — multiplied load on the single registration path, and nobody re-derived the estimate after it.
p1c04.consequence: Six enrollments completed on day one. The site was effectively unusable for roughly two months. GAO found CMS had obligated over $840M against the marketplace and data-hub contracts by March 2014, with later total figures well past $1.7bn; the emergency 'tech surge' that followed became the founding of USDS and 18F.
leads: GAO-14-694, 'Healthcare.gov: Ineffective Planning and Oversight Practices Underscore the Need for Improved Contract Management', July 2014
GAO-15-238, 'Healthcare.gov: CMS Has Taken Steps to Address Problems, but Needs to Further Implement Systems Development Best Practices', 2015
House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform release on the pre-launch load test showing failure at ~1,100 concurrent users
HHS Office of Inspector General, 'CMS Management of the Federal Marketplace: A Case Study', A-18-14-30011, 2016

p1c05.subject: Gene Amdahl argues against Daniel Slotnick's 64-processor ILLIAC IV at the AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, and the machine spends the next eight years proving him right
p1c05.org: University of Illinois / Burroughs / DARPA / NASA Ames (IBM, for Amdahl)
p1c05.why_kernel: The kernel says find the thing that must agree, because that is the real capacity. ILLIAC IV is the purest instance in computing history: 64 processing elements driven by one control unit, so every element had to agree on the instruction. A data-dependent branch idled processors outright. The ceiling was not the number of machines and never could be, and Amdahl proved that in three pages before a wire was laid. Delete this and 'coordination is the ceiling' is an assertion; with it, it is an invoice.
p1c05.struggle: SIMD lockstep meant real programs — the ones with branches — ran at a fraction of the paper 1 GFLOPS. The machine arrived with one quadrant of 64 PEs instead of the planned 256, four years late, and did not run production work reliably until 1975. Campus protest over classified DoD work forced it off the Illinois campus to NASA Ames before it ever ran. Amdahl's serial-fraction argument had no engineering answer, only Gustafson's 1988 rebuttal that you should grow the problem instead.
p1c05.consequence: An $8M 1966 budget became $31M by 1971 delivery, for a machine obsolete on arrival and decommissioned in 1981. Amdahl's three-page AFIPS paper became the law every capacity plan and every scaling argument still obeys, and the reason 'add machines' is a question and not a plan.
leads: Gene M. Amdahl, 'Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities', AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, vol. 30, 1967, pp. 483–485 (DOI 10.1145/1465482.1465560)
W. J. Bouknight et al., 'The Illiac IV System', Proceedings of the IEEE 60(4), April 1972
Daniel Slotnick, 'The Fastest Computer', Scientific American, February 1971
Howard Falk, 'Reaching for a gigaflop', IEEE Spectrum 13(10), October 1976

p1c06.subject: IBM Poughkeepsie ships the first commercial cache — 16KB of monolithic store bolted in front of core memory on the System/360 Model 85 — and coins the word 'cache' for it
p1c06.why_kernel: This is where 'the cache is a suggestion, the store is the truth' was first designed in as a correctness rule rather than discovered as a bug: the Model 85 was required to run existing 360 programs bit-identically whether the cache was present, absent, or empty, so stores were written through to main storage and I/O channel writes invalidated lines — the reader can derive from this one machine why no write may land only in the cache and why invalidation is two systems arguing about one fact.
p1c06.struggle: Transparency only holds while one processor is looking. The moment a channel or a second CPU writes to main storage behind the cache's back, the cache's private copy is a lie the hardware cannot detect on its own — coherence, not speed, becomes the unsolved problem, and the hit ratio itself remains at the mercy of whether the program happens to have locality.
p1c06.consequence: Let IBM sell a machine with an effective storage cycle three to four times faster than the core memory it actually contained, avoiding the cost of building faster core; the Model 85 was a multi-million-dollar system and the store-through-plus-invalidate design propagated into essentially every processor since.
leads: J. S. Liptay, 'Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, II: The cache', IBM Systems Journal 7(1), 1968, pp. 15-21
C. J. Conti, D. H. Gibson, S. H. Pitkowsky, 'Structural aspects of the System/360 Model 85, I: General organization', IBM Systems Journal 7(1), 1968
A. J. Smith, 'Cache Memories', ACM Computing Surveys 14(3), 1982 (survey confirming the 360/85 write-through policy and measured hit ratios)

p1c07.subject: Wikimedia, a donation-funded nonprofit, puts Squid reverse proxies in Amsterdam (then Seoul and Paris) and deliberately strips per-user variation out of anonymous MediaWiki pages so the edge can serve them
p1c07.why_kernel: It is the only case where an organisation changed the product so the bytes could be identical for everyone — MediaWiki was intentionally constrained so an anonymous page renders the same for all readers, which is precisely 'anything identical for everyone should never touch a machine that thinks'. The result is measurable (roughly 85% hit rate on text, 98% on media), so the reader can derive the cache-key rule, the text/media split, and PURGE-on-edit invalidation from one deployment.
p1c07.struggle: Logged-in readers and editors are uncacheable by construction, so the small minority who log in consume almost all the application and database capacity; and one edit to a widely transcluded template fires a purge across millions of pages, making invalidation and the job-queue backlog the real ceiling rather than delivery.
p1c07.consequence: A top-ten global website served from a few hundred servers on a hardware budget in the low single-digit millions, while commercial peers of comparable traffic spent orders of magnitude more; the 2005 cache topology is still the shape of Wikimedia's stack twenty years later.
leads: Mark Bergsma, 'Wikimedia architecture', 2007 slide deck (upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/labs/8/81/Bergsma_-_Wikimedia_architecture_-_2007.pdf)
wikitech.wikimedia.org, 'esams data center' (history of the Amsterdam/knams caching cluster from 2005)
Domas Mituzas, 'Wikipedia: Site internals, configuration, code examples and management issues', MySQL Conference 2007 tutorial

p1c08.subject: After September 11 left clearing banks with backup data centres a few Manhattan blocks from their primaries, the Federal Reserve, SEC and OCC wrote recovery-point and recovery-time objectives and out-of-region backup into US supervisory expectations
p1c08.org: Federal Reserve Board / SEC / OCC (and the clearing banks, notably Bank of New York)
p1c08.why_kernel: This is where 'how far behind is the copy' stopped being an engineering opinion and became a number an examiner checks. The paper forces the reader to see that RPO literally is the replication lag, that a failover taken while a replica is behind is quantified data loss, and — because the regulators pointedly did not mandate synchronous mirroring, only a two-hour recovery expectation and geographic separation — that RPO=0 is bought with latency on every single write.
p1c08.struggle: Distance and RPO=0 are physically incompatible: synchronous mirroring charges a round trip on every commit, so hundreds of miles of mandated separation means accepting a nonzero, measured lag. The agencies could specify neither a distance nor a technology that satisfied both, and the industry argued over the separation guidance for years without resolving it.
p1c08.consequence: Fedwire payment volume fell more than 40% on 11 September 2001 and the Fed injected over $100 billion of liquidity to cover payments that could not be sent; the 2003 paper then forced core clearing and settlement firms to build second, far-away data centres at costs in the hundreds of millions, and put RPO/RTO into every enterprise DR contract since.
leads: 'Interagency Paper on Sound Practices to Strengthen the Resilience of the U.S. Financial System', SEC Release No. 34-47638, 7 April 2003 (also Fed SR 03-9, May 2003) — note it is supervisory guidance, and its explicit numbers are recovery-time (two hours / same business day) plus geographic diversity
Jeffrey M. Lacker, 'Payment System Disruptions and the Federal Reserve Following September 11, 2001', Richmond Fed Working Paper 03-16 (2003); published Journal of Monetary Economics 51(5), 2004
GAO-03-251, 'Potential Terrorist Attacks: Additional Actions Needed to Better Prepare Critical Financial Market Participants', February 2003

p1c09.subject: Taobao's 'favourites' (收藏夹) table — tens of billions of rows that had to be read both by user and by item — could not be sharded on one key, and a small Alibaba team started building OceanBase rather than pick one
p1c09.org: Alibaba / Taobao (team later moved to Ant Group)
p1c09.why_kernel: It is the shard-key dilemma with nothing else in the frame: two dominant reads of equal business value, one key permitted, and whichever you choose the other query becomes a scatter-gather across every machine. The reader derives why the shard key follows the dominant read, and what it costs when there are two dominant reads — a company writes a database.
p1c09.struggle: Their escape hatch was to funnel every recent write through a single in-memory UpdateServer so the sharded read replicas never had to agree — a deliberate one-node ceiling adopted because distributed transactions were out of reach. It took a decade and a Paxos rewrite to remove the very bottleneck the design was built around.
p1c09.consequence: The stopgap became Alipay's production database and the core of Ant's 'de-IOE' programme replacing Oracle; OceanBase later posted the TPC-C record at 707 million tpmC and open-sourced in 2021.
leads: Zhenkun Yang et al., 'OceanBase: A 707 Million tpmC Distributed Relational Database System', PVLDB 15(12), 2022 (vldb.org/pvldb/vol15/p3385-xu.pdf) — see the system-history section, which is the only load-bearing source
'OceanBase Paetica: A Hybrid Shared-nothing/Shared-everything Database', PVLDB 16, 2023
OceanBase 'The architectural evolution of OceanBase Database' (V0.1 for Taobao Favorites, ChunkServer/UpdateServer split, Paxos in 0.5) — vendor-authored, treat as colour

p1c10.subject: David Gifford, building the Violet replicated file system at Xerox PARC, gives every copy a number of votes and requires r + w to exceed the total — inventing the quorum overlap rule
p1c10.why_kernel: R + W > N is not a rule of thumb someone tuned into existence; Gifford derived it as a pigeonhole argument from voting, which is the only way a reader can see that the overlap *is* the guarantee and not a side effect. His paper also carries version numbers on every copy for exactly the reason the kernel's breaks clause names: the overlap proves you saw the newest write, it does not tell you which of the returned copies that is.
p1c10.struggle: The paper's own accounting is the wall: voting makes every read expensive forever in order to survive failures that are rare, the weights must be chosen per file by a human guessing at a failure model, and nobody could say how to choose them. Violet stayed a research system; the knob was shipped without an answer for how to set it.
p1c10.consequence: Thirty years later it is the tunable-consistency dial in Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak and DynamoDB — every QUORUM/ONE/ALL setting an engineer picks is Gifford's r and w, and the 2007 Dynamo paper's sloppy quorums are a direct relaxation of it.
leads: David K. Gifford, 'Weighted Voting for Replicated Data', Proc. 7th ACM SOSP, 1979, pp. 150-162
Xerox PARC technical report CSL-79-14 (bitsavers.org/pdf/xerox/parc/techReports/CSL-79-14_Weighted_Voting_for_Replicated_Data.pdf)
Robert H. Thomas, 'A Majority Consensus Approach to Concurrency Control for Multiple Copy Databases', ACM TODS 4(2), 1979

p1c11.subject: London Ambulance Service Computer Aided Despatch goes live on 26 October 1992 and the queue of unallocated incidents and exception messages grows for two days until the service reverts to paper
p1c11.org: London Ambulance Service / Systems Options Ltd / South West Thames Regional Health Authority
people: John Wilby (LAS Chief Executive, resigned 28 Oct 1992)
p1c11.why_kernel: It is the cleanest proof in the record that a queue does not create capacity: LASCAD converted 'dispatch an ambulance now or fail loudly' into 'enqueue an incident and dispatch eventually', the consumers were a fixed number of physical vehicles slower than the 999 call arrival rate, so the buffer length — not CPU, not the software — was the only number that predicted the collapse, and nobody was watching it.
p1c11.struggle: They could not drain it. Clearing the exception queue to speed the system up lost incidents; lost incidents made callers ring back, which added producers; messages scrolled off the operators' screens faster than they could be read. Every fix inside the software made the arrival rate worse, because the real consumer was an ambulance driving through London and no amount of software makes it arrive faster.
p1c11.consequence: System withdrawn to semi-manual within 36 hours and abandoned entirely on 4 November after a lock-up; response times of up to roughly three hours against a 14-minute standard; the Chief Executive resigned on 28 October; a contract awarded at about £1.1-1.5m against a written-off programme of several million pounds; press and inquiry testimony alleged deaths, which the February 1993 inquiry declined to attribute but did not rule out.
leads: Report of the Inquiry Into The London Ambulance Service, South West Thames Regional Health Authority, February 1993 (ISBN 0-905133-70-6) — full text at www0.cs.ucl.ac.uk/staff/A.Finkelstein/las/lascase0.9.pdf
Hansard, House of Commons, 28 October 1992, 'London Ambulance Service'
A. Finkelstein and J. Dowell, 'A Comedy of Errors: the London Ambulance Service case study', IWSSD-8, 1996

p1c12.subject: The ATM Forum and ITU-T settle the Generic Cell Rate Algorithm as the way to police a traffic contract — one counter, one clock read, one verdict per 53-byte cell at 353,000 cells per second (ITU-T I.371; ATM Forum UNI 3.1, 1994)
p1c12.org: ATM Forum / ITU-T Study Group 13 / carrier equipment vendors
people: Jonathan S. Turner (named the leaky bucket, 1986)
ITU-T SG13 / ATM Forum Traffic Management working group
p1c12.why_kernel: This is where the four algorithms in the chapter stopped being folklore and became a spec: at 353k decisions per second in silicon you cannot keep a log of timestamps, so the committee was forced down to literally one counter and one clock reading, and I.371 then writes the same algorithm twice — as a virtual scheduling algorithm (theoretical arrival time, constant drain) and as a continuous-state leaky bucket (continuous refill) — and proves they are equivalent, which is exactly the kernel's claim that what resets the counter *is* the choice of algorithm.
p1c12.struggle: Cell delay variation. Traffic that left the customer perfectly conforming arrives at the policer jittered by multiplexing across intermediate switches, so the algorithm needs a tolerance term τ (CDVT) — and there is no principled way to pick it. Too tight and you discard cells from a customer who obeyed the contract and then bill them for it; too loose and the contract polices nothing. The parameter was never solved, only negotiated.
p1c12.consequence: Every ATM traffic contract (PCR, SCR, MBS, CDVT) and every CLP-tagging carrier SLA of the 1990s hung on this one algorithm; a wrongly-tuned τ meant a carrier silently discarding a paying customer's traffic and losing the resulting dispute. The unfixable tuning problem is part of why per-flow policing lost to IP's dumb best-effort core, and the algorithm survived anyway — RFCs 2697/2698 are the same buckets re-badged for IP, and it is the token bucket sitting in every API gateway today.
leads: ITU-T Recommendation I.371, 'Traffic control and congestion control in B-ISDN' — Generic Cell Rate Algorithm / Usage Parameter Control (first published 1991, revised 1996): the two equivalent flowcharts
ATM Forum, 'ATM User-Network Interface Specification, Version 3.1' (September 1994), UPC/GCRA section
J. S. Turner, 'New Directions in Communications (or Which Way to the Information Age?)', IEEE Communications Magazine 24(10), October 1986 — the origin of the leaky bucket

p1c13.subject: IBM builds ICS/DL/I (later IMS) for North American Rockwell in 1966-68 to answer one question about the Saturn V — what parts go into this assembly — and installs it in August 1968; the hierarchy that made that walk cheap is the reason Codd writes his 1970 paper
p1c13.org: North American Rockwell (Apollo command module and Saturn V second stage) / IBM / NASA
p1c13.why_kernel: It is the origin of the whole trade the chapter teaches, at full scale and with the receipts still visible: a two-million-part bill of materials is a tree, so IMS hard-coded the tree as physical parent-child pointers, made that one traversal absurdly cheap, and made literally every other question require a new program — which is the kernel's second half ('everything else expensive') and its Breaks clause ('when the access pattern changes after launch') proved over fifty-plus years rather than one quarter. It also reframes the chapter's real claim: NoSQL did not invent access-path-bound storage, it re-adopted it, and Codd is the argument the reader is unknowingly re-running in the design review.
p1c13.struggle: The pointers are the schema. Once the access path is in the data, a new question is not a new query, it is a new program and often a new physical layout — and the organisations that ran IMS could not stop running it long enough to change it. Codd's paper is not a triumph in this story; it is the diagnosis that took another decade of committee fighting (the 1974 Codd–Bachman debate) to be believed, while the installed base kept growing.
p1c13.consequence: IMS shipped commercially in 1968 and is still in production in 2020s core banking, insurance and airline systems — IBM cites it carrying the transaction volume of most of the Fortune 1000 — which means the access pattern chosen for a moon-rocket parts list in 1966 is still setting the cost of every core-system replacement programme, the ones that regularly run past nine figures and get cancelled.
leads: K. R. Blackman, 'Technical note: IMS celebrates thirty years as an IBM product', IBM Systems Journal 37(4), 1998
E. F. Codd, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks', Communications of the ACM 13(6), June 1970
C. W. Bachman, 'The Programmer as Navigator', 1973 ACM Turing Award Lecture, CACM 16(11), November 1973 — and the Codd/Bachman exchange at ACM SIGFIDET 1974

p1c14.subject: Spring 1999: Richard M. Smith shows that every Office 97 document carries a version-1 UUID with the creating machine's Ethernet MAC address inside it, fingerprints the Melissa virus document against earlier 'VicodinES' files, and Microsoft ships a patch to strip the identifier
p1c14.org: Microsoft / Open Software Foundation DCE lineage (Apollo Computer NCS) / IETF / FBI
people: Paul J. Leach (UUID spec, ex-Apollo Computer)
p1c14.why_kernel: It shows what 'uniqueness without coordination' actually had to buy the bits with. A v1 UUID could not be unique from 128 random bits alone in 1988 hardware, so it borrowed the only globally-administered unique number already on the machine — the IEEE-assigned MAC — plus a 100ns clock, plus a clock_sequence field whose entire reason for existing is that a backwards clock reissues IDs. That is Snowflake's machine-id + timestamp + sequence, twenty years early, and this event is where the hidden third price of the trade got itemised in public: the coordination you skipped is still encoded in the ID, and it is readable by anyone holding one.
p1c14.struggle: Both ways out cost something the chapter's readers will pay again. Going random (v4) killed the leak and killed index locality with it — 128 bits scattered across a B-tree. Keeping the timestamp in front to get the locality back (v7, RFC 9562, 2024) hands the creation time to every recipient and re-inherits the clock-skew failure that clock_seq was invented to paper over. Twenty-five years of standards work has moved the cost around, not removed it.
p1c14.consequence: Melissa cost an estimated $80m+ in cleanup across US business (GAO testimony, April 1999); its author drew 20 months federal prison and a $5,000 fine. Microsoft shipped an Office 97 identifier-removal patch and stopped embedding the MAC — a forced change to the file format of the world's most-used document product. RFC 4122 (2005) codified the warning; RFC 9562 (May 2024) finally deprecates MAC-derived node IDs.
leads: RFC 4122, 'A Universally Unique IDentifier (UUID) URN Namespace' (2005), §4.1.5-4.1.6 and §6; superseded by RFC 9562 (May 2024)
P. J. Leach and R. Salz, 'UUIDs and GUIDs', IETF Internet-Draft, February 1998 — the Apollo NCS / OSF DCE lineage of the 128-bit format

GAO testimony T-AIMD-99-146, 'Information Security: The Melissa Computer Virus Demonstrates Urgent Need for Stronger Protection', 15 April 1999; plus the March-April 1999 Microsoft Office 'Unique Identifier' patch and Richard M. Smith's contemporaneous disclosure

p2c01.subject: The collapse of Bankhaus Herstatt, Cologne, 26 June 1974 — the German regulator pulled its licence at 16:30 CET, after counterparties had paid Deutschmarks in Frankfurt that morning and before Herstatt's New York correspondent released the matching dollars; the loss became the permanent industry name for the problem ("Herstatt risk") and, 28 years later, CLS's payment-versus-payment coordinator
p2c01.org: Bankhaus I.D. Herstatt / Bundesaufsichtsamt für das Kreditwesen / BIS-CPSS / CLS Bank
people: Morten Bech (BIS, FX settlement risk measurement)
p2c01.why_kernel: Two banks, two national payment systems, one trade: the DM leg committed in Frankfurt and the dollar leg never landed, so the reader can derive that 'atomic across two systems' is never a property you inherit — it is a coordinator somebody has to build and pay for — and that when the industry finally built it (CLS's PvP), it blocks with pay-in deadlines and a five-hour window in exactly the way 2PC's theory says a coordinator must.
p2c01.struggle: The fix is a real two-phase commit at industry scale, and it inherits 2PC's costs rather than escaping them: CLS only works during the narrow window when every relevant RTGS system is simultaneously open, members must pre-fund by hard deadlines, and it covers only 18 currencies — so fifty years after Herstatt a large share of daily FX turnover still settles the old way, because you cannot compel every participant to join the coordinator.
p2c01.consequence: Counterparties lost the paid-in DM leg outright — roughly $620M in-flight at 1974 values, with the New York clearing system seizing up behind it; the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision was created within months as a direct response, and the eventual engineering answer, CLS, did not go live until 2002. BIS still measured trillions of dollars a day settling without PvP as of its 2019 and 2025 surveys.
leads: BIS/CPSS, 'Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions' (the Allsopp Report), March 1996
Bech & Holden, 'FX settlement risk remains significant', BIS Quarterly Review, December 2019
Bank of England archive files on the June 1974 Herstatt closure, surveyed in Bank Underground, 24 June 2015
BCBS, 'Supervisory Guidance for Managing Settlement Risk in Foreign Exchange Transactions', September 2000

p2c02.subject: The Post Office Horizon scandal, UK, 1999–2024 — Fujitsu/ICL Pathway's branch accounting system, whose retried and duplicated transactions (the Dalmellington bug: one frozen screen, repeated keypresses, three £8,000 transfers instead of one) and Riposte replication defects (the Callendar Square/Falkirk lock bug) produced phantom shortfalls that subpostmasters were held personally, then criminally, liable for
p2c02.org: Post Office Ltd / Fujitsu (ICL Pathway) / Escher Group (Riposte)
p2c02.why_kernel: The terminal retried and the central datastore recorded each retry as a fresh effect, so the reader watches the gap between exactly-once delivery and exactly-once effect turn into a criminal conviction — and then derives the two clauses that matter: the dedup record must live in the same transaction as the effect, and a ledger that the party liable for it cannot read, and that the vendor can silently amend, is not append-only and therefore not a ledger.
p2c02.struggle: The books balanced. Double-entry was satisfied because every phantom entry had a counterpart, so no internal invariant fired; the branch had no read access to its own transaction history, no way to reconcile against anything outside Horizon, and Fujitsu retained an undisclosed ability to inject and amend branch transactions remotely. The invariant a ledger can check is internal consistency, never truth — and the Post Office treated the ledger as the external source of truth about cash it had never counted.
p2c02.consequence: Over 900 subpostmasters prosecuted (most by the Post Office's own private prosecutions), 236 imprisoned, at least four suicides linked to the shortfalls, thousands more bankrupted paying back money that never went missing; convictions quashed in blocks from 2021, blanket statutory exoneration under the Post Office (Horizon System Offences) Act 2024, and well over £1bn in compensation — the largest miscarriage of justice in English legal history.
leads: Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd (No. 6: Horizon Issues) [2019] EWHC 3408 (QB), Fraser J, 16 December 2019 — and Appendix 1, the schedule of bugs (Callendar Square/Falkirk, Dalmellington, Receipts and Payments Mismatch, Suspense Account)
Second Sight, 'Interim Report into alleged problems with the Horizon system', 8 July 2013
Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry (Sir Wyn Williams), Fujitsu witness statements and transcripts on remote access, 2022–2024
Hamilton & Ors v Post Office Ltd [2021] EWCA Crim 577 (39 convictions quashed as an abuse of process)

p2c03.subject: The Abermule head-on collision, Cambrian Railways, Montgomeryshire, Wales, 26 January 1921 — two trains entered the same single-line section while Tyer's electric train tablet apparatus, a correct interlocked mutual-exclusion device in use since the 1870s, was working perfectly; the driver took a tablet nobody checked and never read the section name stamped on it
p2c03.org: Cambrian Railways / Ministry of Transport Railway Inspectorate / Tyer & Co.
people: Colonel Sir John Pringle (Ministry of Transport inspecting officer)
Lord Herbert Vane-Tempest (Cambrian Railways director, killed in the crash)
p2c03.why_kernel: The paired tablet instruments are a physical two-node consensus device — electrically interlocked so at most one tablet for a section can be out at a time — and 17 people still died, which is the cleanest available proof of the kernel's named boundary: holding the lock is only a statement about the past, and the grant is worthless unless the token itself is inspected at the resource, at the moment of use, by the thing about to act.
p2c03.struggle: The protocol could not be improved, because the protocol was not what failed. Every party who touched the tablet — signalman, porter, stationmaster, driver — was a place to skip the check, and the inquiry's fix was not a better lock but a rule about where the check must happen: the tablet is handled only by the signalman, and the driver must read the section name on it before entering. You cannot push the check into the lock; it has to live at the resource, on the last actor, every single time.
p2c03.consequence: 17 dead and 36 injured, still the worst single-line collision in British railway history; four Cambrian employees dismissed; the Ministry of Transport report rewrote tablet-handling rules across the network, and Abermule became the standard teaching case in British signalling practice for the next century.
leads: Ministry of Transport, 'Report on the Collision at Abermule on 26th January 1921', Colonel Sir John Pringle, 1921 (Railways Archive doc 103)
Hansard, HC Deb 28 February 1921, 'Railway Accident, Abermule'
Regulation of Railways Act 1889 (absolute block working and interlocking made compulsory after Armagh — the statute that put the token system there)

p2c04.subject: The Nancy disproofs, 2003–2006 — Imine, Molli, Oster and Rusinowitch at LORIA/INRIA fed the published, peer-reviewed operational-transformation functions into an automated theorem prover, which returned counterexamples showing they violated TP2 and diverged; the same group then abandoned transformation entirely and published WOOT at CSCW 2006, the first sequence CRDT and the direct ancestor of Yjs and Automerge
p2c04.org: LORIA / INRIA Nancy-Grand Est (ECOO team), France
people: Clarence Ellis and Simon Gibbs (dOPT, SIGMOD 1989)
p2c04.why_kernel: The chapter's two branches are usually presented as a taste question; this story shows they are a causal sequence. The reader watches a machine produce concrete three-operation counterexamples where two clients running a published OT algorithm converge to *different* documents, and then watches the authors of the disproof conclude that the only escape is to design the data so order cannot matter — CRDTs exist because rewriting operations turned out to be too subtle for humans to get right, not because anyone preferred them.
p2c04.struggle: The escape is bought, not free. WOOT gives every character a globally unique identity that is never reused, which means deletions become tombstones and the document only ever grows — the fix for divergence is a data structure that cannot shrink. And neither branch touches the thing users actually complain about: both OT and CRDT converge, and neither notices that the merged sentence is nonsense. Convergence is not intent preservation.
p2c04.consequence: Roughly fifteen years of published transformation functions — dOPT (1989), adOPTed, SOCT2, GOTO, SDT — invalidated by counterexample, with the field's central correctness condition (TP2) shown to be unsatisfiable for the obvious string model; the downstream effect is the entire offline-first branch of the industry: WOOT → Logoot/LSEQ/Treedoc/RGA → Yjs, Automerge, Riak's data types, and every peer-to-peer editor that ships today without a sequencing server.
leads: Imine, Molli, Oster, Rusinowitch, 'Proving Correctness of Transformation Functions in Real-Time Groupware', ECSCW 2003 (SPIKE theorem prover; HAL inria-00107652)
Oster, Urso, Molli, Imine, 'Data Consistency for P2P Collaborative Editing', ACM CSCW 2006 (WOOT — the first sequence CRDT)
Ellis & Gibbs, 'Concurrency Control in Groupware Systems', ACM SIGMOD 1989 (the dOPT transformation later shown incorrect)
Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero, Zawirski, 'A Comprehensive Study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types', INRIA RR-7506, 2011

p2c05.subject: The AT&T long-distance network collapse, 15 January 1990 — a defect in the SS7 recovery code loaded onto all 114 #4ESS toll switches turned a single switch's routine reset in New York into a self-sustaining nationwide cascade; every switch in the country cycled on roughly six-second reboots for nine hours
p2c05.org: AT&T Long Lines / Bell Labs / FCC Common Carrier Bureau
people: Peter G. Neumann (ACM RISKS Forum, contemporaneous technical account)
Robert Allen (AT&T chairman, public apology and discount day)
p2c05.why_kernel: One hundred and fourteen switches, fully meshed, all running one software load, is a system with exactly one cell — so the reader can derive both halves of the kernel from a single event: why you cut a fleet into cells with a boundary failure cannot cross, and why the shared thing every cell depends on (here the common SS7 control plane and the uniform release) is precisely what un-cells you. It is the ur-case for 'most large outages are the one component everybody depended on'.
p2c05.struggle: The recovery mechanism was the propagation mechanism. A switch coming back healthy is what crashed its neighbours, so every instinct — restart it, bring it back faster — made the cascade stronger. There was no way to fence off a region because the network's whole value was that every switch talked to every other. The engineers' only working move was to shed load until the oscillation damped, then roll back to the previous software release; and the defect had passed AT&T's testing, because it only appears under timing that exists at network scale.
p2c05.consequence: About nine hours of nationwide outage; roughly half of AT&T's long-distance call attempts blocked, tens of millions of calls lost, an estimated $60M+ in forgone revenue plus knock-on losses to airlines, hotels and catalogue retailers whose 800-numbers were the network; AT&T ran a public discount day, and the FCC opened the network-reliability inquiries that led to the industry's outage-reporting regime.
leads: Peter G. Neumann, 'Cause of AT&T network failure', ACM RISKS Digest Vol. 9 Issues 62–63, January 1990 — and Neumann, Computer-Related Risks (ACM Press, 1995), §2.1
'Why the AT&T network crashed', Telephony, 22 January 1990 — the misplaced break in the do-while in the 4ESS recovery code
AT&T's filing and the FCC Common Carrier Bureau inquiry into the 15 January 1990 outage, and the subsequent Network Reliability Council reports

p2c06.subject: The Bloodbath of B-R5RB, EVE Online, 27–28 January 2014 — 7,548 pilots converged on one solar system, which in EVE's architecture is one process on one core; CCP could not shard it, so they ran the fight for 21 hours at as low as 10% simulation speed under Time Dilation. It started because one director missed a routine sovereignty bill
people: CCP's performance team (dev-blog handle 'CCP Veritas', author of the Time Dilation blogs)
the N3/Pandemic Legion director whose missed station bill opened the system to capture
p2c06.why_kernel: EVE shards its entire universe by solar system — a perfect partition key with tens of thousands of keys — and one key still ate a whole machine, because traffic followed the players and not the hash. The reader derives directly that the hot-key toolkit is isolation and admission control rather than better sharding, and hits the boundary clause in the same story: CCP could not split B-R5RB across nodes, because everything inside a system must interact and splitting the key destroys the ordering and atomicity that *is* the simulation.
p2c06.struggle: CCP never solved single-system scaling and still has not. The two available moves are both admissions: reinforce the node (move that one key onto dedicated hardware, which players have to request in advance, so the fix requires knowing which key will go hot before it does), and Time Dilation — slow the clock for everyone inside the hot key until the queue drains. Twenty-one hours at one-tenth speed is not a fix; it is graceful degradation dressed as a feature, and it is the honest ceiling on one key on one machine.
p2c06.consequence: 75 titans, 13 supercarriers, 370 dreadnoughts and 123 carriers destroyed — around 11 trillion ISK, roughly $300,000 of real-money-equivalent, the most costly single engagement in the game's history; 6,058 pilots in one system with 2,670 concurrent at peak, and a 21-hour battle that most participants experienced as a slideshow.
leads: CCP Games, 'The Bloodbath of B-R5RB' official battle report, 2014 (destruction totals, 7,548 unique pilots, 21-hour duration)
CCP dev blogs on Time Dilation — 'Time Dilation aka TiDi' (2011) and the CCP Veritas performance follow-ups on per-solar-system nodes and node reinforcement
CCP's GDC / Nordic Game talks on EVE's single-shard Tranquility cluster and Stackless Python architecture
CBS News and GameSpot, 28 January 2014, ~$300,000 in destroyed ships

p2c07.subject: The October 1986 Internet congestion collapse — throughput between LBL and UC Berkeley, two buildings 400 yards apart, fell from 32 kbps to 40 bps — and John Nagle's proof a year earlier (RFC 970) that a switch with infinite buffers doesn't avoid collapse, it guarantees it
p2c07.why_kernel: RFC 970's result is the kernel stated as a theorem — infinite storage, FIFO queueing, and a finite packet lifetime means that under overload every packet is eventually dropped anyway, after the sender has already given up and retransmitted, so the buffer converted an honest immediate refusal into a slow refusal that cost the network all its capacity; delete this and the reader has no reason to believe that a bounded queue is safer than a big one, and no origin for Little's Law, timeouts-with-backoff, retry storms or the whole shed-early doctrine.
p2c07.struggle: The network has no channel to say 'stop': the only backpressure signal available is a dropped packet, indistinguishable from a broken link, so senders must infer overload from loss. The explicit alternative, ICMP Source Quench, was tried and eventually deprecated outright (RFC 6633, 2012) because sending a 'slow down' message costs more than dropping — and two decades later cheap RAM re-hid the signal under oversized buffers (bufferbloat, Gettys 2010).
p2c07.consequence: A 1000x throughput collapse on affected paths and a series of repeat collapses across ARPANET/NSFNET through 1986-87 that nearly made the research internet unusable; the fixes (slow start, congestion avoidance, RTT-variance-based RTO, fast retransmit) shipped in 4.3BSD Tahoe and now run on essentially every TCP connection in existence.
leads: RFC 970, John Nagle, 'On Packet Switches With Infinite Storage', December 1985
Van Jacobson & Michael J. Karels, 'Congestion Avoidance and Control', ACM SIGCOMM 1988 (ee.lbl.gov/papers/congavoid.pdf)
RFC 896, John Nagle, 'Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks', January 1984

p2c08.subject: Three Mile Island Unit 2, 28 March 1979 — over 100 alarms in the first minutes, an alarm printer running two and a half hours behind, and the one indicator that mattered showing that a close command had been sent to the pilot-operated relief valve rather than whether the valve had actually closed
p2c08.org: Metropolitan Edison / GPU; President's Commission on the Accident at TMI (Kemeny Commission); US NRC
p2c08.why_kernel: The PORV light instrumented the plant's intent, not the plant's effect — the exact failure mode of alerting on CPU, queue depth or deploy success instead of on the thing the user experiences — and the 100-alarm flood is the proof that the fix is not more signals but one prioritized signal tied to the outcome; delete it and 'pick the number the user feels' is an aphorism instead of a lesson with a control room behind it, and the chapter loses the argument for symptom-based paging and for the kernel's own break clause (a rare catastrophic event is not a budget line).
p2c08.struggle: You cannot alarm your way to understanding, and nobody has fixed it since. The industry's own guidance, EEMUA 191 (1999), sets a steady-state target of roughly one alarm per operator per ten minutes; surveys of real process plants routinely find rates an order of magnitude or two above that, and alarm flooding remains a live cause in modern process incidents.
p2c08.consequence: Roughly $1B and fourteen years to clean up the damaged core; the utility effectively destroyed; and no new US nuclear plant construction start for about three decades. The Kemeny Report explicitly refused to blame the operators and put the fault on control room design, training and the NRC.
leads: Report of the President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island (Kemeny Report), October 1979
NUREG/KM-0001, 'Three Mile Island Accident of 1979 Knowledge Management Digest', US NRC
EEMUA Publication 191, 'Alarm Systems: A Guide to Design, Management and Procurement', 1st edition 1999

p2c09.subject: Japan Meteorological Agency's earthquake early warning system in the two months after the 11 March 2011 Tohoku quake: 44 of the 70 public warnings issued were wrong, and over 70% of those failures came from the algorithm associating arrivals from two concurrent aftershocks into one event
p2c09.org: Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA); Kyoto University DPRI
p2c09.why_kernel: EEW is a stream processor with the dial cranked to its physical limit: seismic arrivals reach stations in distance order (late, out of order, by definition), and every extra second of waiting for stragglers buys magnitude accuracy and costs warning time — so the system must literally declare 'I stop waiting now', assign each late arrival to a window, and issue retractions when it was wrong; the aftershock sequence is the clean proof that the whole failure mode is window assignment, not throughput. Delete it and watermarks read as a Flink configuration knob rather than as the one declaration everything else in the chapter follows from.
p2c09.struggle: There is no cutoff that is correct for two overlapping events. Waiting longer resolves the ambiguity and destroys the warning; cutting sooner keeps the warning and mislabels the data. The 2014 IPF (integrated particle filter) work and later PLUM only moved the trade, they did not remove it, and JMA took until 2016-2018 to get the replacements into production.
p2c09.consequence: Weeks of false and missed public alerts to a population that had just lost ~18,000 people, with the credibility of the whole warning system at stake; JMA re-architected the association algorithm (IPF, then PLUM) over the following five to seven years.
leads: Hoshiba & Ozaki, 'Earthquake Early Warning and Tsunami Warning of the Japan Meteorological Agency, and their Performance in the 2011 Off the Pacific Coast of Tohoku Earthquake' (Springer, 2012)
Liu & Yamada, 'Multi-events earthquake early warning algorithm using a Bayesian approach', Geophysical Journal International 200(2):791-808, 2014
