p2c10.subject: Doug McIlroy fitting a 30,000-word spelling dictionary into a PDP-11's 64KB address space for Unix spell — first with a 400,000-bit superimposed-code (Bloom) filter of 11 hash functions accepting one nonword in 2,000, then throwing that filter away when the word list grew and replacing it with Golomb-coded hash differences at 13.60 bits per word against a 13.57-bit theoretical floor
p2c10.org: Bell Labs (Computing Science Research Center), Murray Hill
p2c10.why_kernel: This is the kernel executed in both halves and then failing: McIlroy traded exactness for space, and he could ship it only because the error ran in the tolerable direction — a false positive means one misspelling slips past, never a correct word flagged, so no writer is ever contradicted by the tool — and then the trade broke on him, because the false-positive rate is a function of n/m and rises silently as the dictionary grows. Delete it and the reader gets 'Bloom filters have false positives' as a property list, not the two things they must actually do: name which way the error runs before adopting the structure, and re-derive the rate every time the data grows.
p2c10.struggle: You cannot tune your way out of a filled Bloom filter. Growing the list from 25,000 to 30,000 words demanded a bigger bit table than the machine had, there is no deletion and no rescaling in place, and the resolution was to abandon the probabilistic structure entirely for exact compression — the sketch was not the endpoint, it was the thing that ran out.
p2c10.consequence: The alternative was a disk-resident dictionary on a shared PDP-11, which meant spell could not be an interactive one-pass filter at all; the technique McIlroy landed on shipped in v7 through v10 Unix and stood for a decade, and the same Bloom/Golomb pairing is what every LSM storage engine and every compact block filter reaches for now.
leads: M. D. McIlroy, 'Development of a Spelling List', IEEE Transactions on Communications 30(1):91-99, January 1982
Burton H. Bloom, 'Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors', CACM 13(7):422-426, July 1970
v10 Unix spell source, github.com/arnoldrobbins/v10spell

p2c11.subject: TSB's big-bang cutover of 5.4 million customers off Lloyds' platform onto Sabadell's Proteo4UK over the weekend of 22 April 2018 — reader and writer moved in the same instant, with no way back
p2c11.org: TSB Bank plc / Banco Sabadell (SABIS); FCA and PRA
p2c11.why_kernel: TSB is the counter-proof the kernel is built out of: they did in one deploy what the chapter says takes four, so there was no phase that reverted independently, no dual-write period to fall back to, and no shadow-read comparison that could have caught the divergence before customers were on the new store — and the moment real transactions landed on the new platform, going back would have meant discarding customer money movements, which is why the answer to 'just roll it back' was silence for eight months. Delete it and 'four deploys, never two' is an assertion; with it, the reader can derive each phase from the specific rollback that phase preserves.
p2c11.struggle: The wall is that a migration's rollback window closes the instant the new system takes a write the old one never saw — and that the deadline was commercial, not technical: TSB was paying Lloyds for the old platform under a transitional agreement, so the cutover date was set by a contract and the go/no-go decision had no honest 'no' left in it.
p2c11.consequence: Roughly £330M of incident and remediation cost on top of £318M of migration spend, a £107.4M statutory pre-tax loss for 2018, 33,101 complaints in the first ten days (a 1,156% jump), fraud attacks peaking at ~70x normal three weeks later, eight months to full resolution, the CEO's resignation, and a £48.65M FCA/PRA fine in December 2022.
leads: FCA Final Notice, TSB Bank plc, 20 December 2022 (and the parallel PRA Final Notice)
Slaughter and May, 'Independent Review of TSB's 2018 Migration' (published 2022)
House of Commons Treasury Committee, 'IT Failures in the Financial Services Sector', HC 224, October 2019

p3c01.subject: The ISBN: Gordon Foster's 9-digit Standard Book Number for W.H. Smith (1965-66), its promotion to the 10-digit ISO 2108 ISBN (1970), and the global forced migration to 13 digits on 1 January 2007 when the 10-digit namespace ran out
p3c01.org: W.H. Smith / Whitaker & Sons / International ISBN Agency / ISO TC46
p3c01.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is a four-way ID tradeoff — unique, short, mintable without a central 'next number please' service, non-guessable — and ISBN is the same problem solved once, in public, with the arithmetic visible: the alphabet was chosen for what a barcode scanner and a human transcriber can survive, the width was chosen by a capacity estimate that later proved wrong, the check digit exists because a silent collision ships the wrong book to the wrong buyer, and coordination-free minting was bought exactly the way Snowflake buys it — coordinate once, at prefix-block assignment, then let each publisher mint locally forever. Delete this story and the reader can still recite 'use base62 with a pre-allocated range'; they cannot derive why the range allocator is the answer, why the check digit is not optional, or why '7 characters is enough forever' is a claim with a due date. Honest gap: ISBN does not derive property (d), unguessability.
p3c01.struggle: Variable-length registrant blocks meant the space was consumed by block hoarding and mis-sizing, not by book volume; by 2005 the English-language registration groups were exhausted. There is no way to widen an identifier in place under readers you do not control, so the entire world had to change primary key on one calendar date, and ISBN-10 and ISBN-13 still coexist in library and retail databases twenty years later.
p3c01.consequence: Every publisher, wholesaler, library catalogue, barcode plate and point-of-sale system on earth was re-plumbed to a single deadline of 1 Jan 2007 (ISO 2108:2005, 'Bookland' EAN-13 prefixes 978/979); duplicate and re-used ISBNs shipped wrong titles to buyers for decades before that.
leads: Gordon Foster, 'The Standard Book Numbering System' — report to W.H. Smith & Son, 1966 (reproduced by the International ISBN Agency)
ISO 2108:2005, Information and documentation — International Standard Book Number, 4th edition
ISO news item, 'Why did ISBN users begin making New Year 2007 resolutions in 2005?', October 2006
BISG ISBN-13 Transition guidelines (2004-2006) and Library of Congress CDS notice on ISBN-13

p3c02.subject: T9 predictive text: Tegic Communications shipping a frequency-ranked, read-only word dictionary in a handset's ROM (1995-1999), because a 1990s phone had no network, no disk and kilobytes of RAM in which to search at keypress time
p3c02.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is 'the ranking must already be done before the request arrives; the read path is one lookup into an immutable dictionary.' T9 is that sentence with the escape hatches physically removed: an 8-bit handset CPU with tens of kilobytes of ROM, no network, and a hard budget of one keypress means request-time search is not merely slow, it is impossible — so the digit sequence becomes a key into a pre-sorted, pre-ranked, compressed, read-only table built offline from a corpus, and shipped frozen. A reader who has this can derive why the deployed artifact is a hash-lookup dictionary rather than a live trie, why builds are atomic swaps rather than in-place updates, and why personalisation has to be a tiny separate layer bolted on top of an immutable base — none of which is derivable from 'precompute is faster'.
p3c02.struggle: A frozen frequency-ranked list cannot learn. 4663 is 'good', 'home', 'gone', 'hood' and 'hone' in an order the corpus picked and the user cannot argue with; a word not in the ROM did not exist; the per-device user dictionary added to fix this was tiny, unranked and lost on reset — the exact ceiling the chapter's read-only dictionary has, discovered by a billion people one keypress at a time.
p3c02.consequence: AOL bought Tegic in December 1999 for roughly $300M in stock; T9 shipped on billions of handsets across Nokia, Motorola, Samsung and Siemens, and its disambiguation errors became the defining text-entry experience of a decade — the reason 'textonyms' has a name.
leads: US Patent 5,818,437, 'Reduced keyboard disambiguating computer', Grover, King & Kushler, filed 1995, granted 6 Oct 1998 (assigned to Tegic)
I. S. MacKenzie & R. W. Soukoreff, 'Text Entry for Mobile Computing: Models and Methods, Theory and Practice', Human-Computer Interaction 17 (2002)
AOL/Tegic acquisition announcement and SEC filings, November-December 1999
Silfverberg, MacKenzie & Korhonen, 'Predicting text entry speed on mobile phones', CHI 2000

p3c03.subject: Alarm fatigue: the January 2010 death of an 89-year-old cardiac patient at Massachusetts General Hospital while his monitor's crisis alarm was switched off and ten nurses heard none of the lower-priority alarms, leading to Joint Commission Sentinel Event Alert 50 (8 April 2013) and a National Patient Safety Goal on alarm management
p3c03.org: Massachusetts General Hospital / The Joint Commission / ECRI Institute
p3c03.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is that exactly-once delivery to a human endpoint is impossible, that every notification must pass per-user gates, and that the real engineering decision is which failure you accept per priority class. A hospital ward is that system with the abstraction stripped off: 85-99% of alarm signals require no clinical action, several hundred fire per patient per day, and the gates — default thresholds, per-bed suppression, escalation, volume — are all real, all tunable, and all lethal in both directions. Turning the crisis alarm off on one bed is a per-user preference that made a P0 undeliverable; leaving every alarm on is a rate-limit failure that made every P0 invisible. A reader who has this derives why dedup and preference gates must run before delivery, why P0 must bypass quiet hours, and above all why the failure mode is not 'the message was lost' but 'the channel was destroyed by the messages that didn't matter'.
p3c03.struggle: There is no threshold that fixes it. Tightening alarms restores signal but silences a real event you cannot identify in advance; loosening them guarantees you deliver everything and the human stops listening. Twelve years after the alert, alarm hazards were still on ECRI's top-ten list — the gates are necessary and provably insufficient, which is the chapter's honest ending.
p3c03.consequence: 98 alarm-related events reported to the Joint Commission Jan 2009-Jun 2012 produced 80 deaths and 13 permanent losses of function; MGH settled with the family for $850,000; alarm management became NPSG.06.01.01, binding on every accredited US hospital from 2014, and ECRI ranked alarm hazards its #1 health technology hazard for four straight years.
leads: The Joint Commission, Sentinel Event Alert Issue 50, 'Medical device alarm safety in hospitals', 8 April 2013
Liz Kowalczyk, 'Patient alarms often unheard, unheeded', Boston Globe, 13 February 2011 (and 'Alarm fatigue linked to heart patient's death at Mass. General', 3 April 2010)
CMS/DPH investigation findings into the January 2010 MGH death; settlement reported November 2011
AAMI/FDA/TJC/ACCE 2011 Clinical Alarms Summit report; ECRI Top 10 Health Technology Hazards 2012-2015

p3c04.subject: RFC 1047, 'Duplicate messages and SMTP' (Craig Partridge, BBN, February 1988): mail relays that had durably accepted a message but were slow to emit the 250 reply caused senders to time out and resend, so the ARPANET/CSNET mail system generated duplicates by design — and the fix became the SMTP timeout floors written into RFC 1123
p3c04.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is a ladder of acknowledgments, each rung a promise from a distinct party, plus retries that are safe to repeat — and 'persist before you ack'. RFC 1047 names the gap precisely: between the moment the receiving mailer decides to accept the message and the moment the sending mailer sees 250, the message is live at both ends, so a lost ack is indistinguishable from a lost message and the only safe sender behaviour produces duplicates. That is the entire single-tick problem, stated in three pages in 1988, by a party who could not add a client-generated message id to close it and had to legislate timeouts instead. It also gives the reader the rest of the ladder for free and honestly: SMTP 250 is the server tick, DSN (RFC 3461) is the delivered tick, and MDN (RFC 3798/8098) is the read tick — advisory, unenforceable, routinely refused, which is exactly what a blue tick actually is.
p3c04.struggle: The gap cannot be closed by the protocol. Partridge could only ask receivers to shrink the window and ask senders to wait longer; the real fix — a sender-minted identity the receiver dedups on — had to be pushed out to Message-ID matching at the endpoint, which nobody is obliged to implement. Email still delivers duplicates today for exactly the reason written down in 1988.
p3c04.consequence: The specific SMTP timeout floors in RFC 1123 §5.3.2 (October 1989) — including the 10-minute wait for the reply after end-of-data — exist because of this failure, and they are the reason a stuck mail server holds your connection for ten minutes rather than retrying into a duplicate storm; the same reasoning later produced RFC 1845's checkpoint/restart extension attempt.
leads: RFC 1047, 'Duplicate messages and SMTP', C. Partridge, February 1988
RFC 1123 §5.3.2, 'Requirements for Internet Hosts — Application and Support', October 1989 (SMTP timeouts)
RFC 5321 §4.1.1.4 and §6.1: the receiver must take responsibility for delivery before returning 250
RFC 3798 / RFC 8098 (Message Disposition Notification) and RFC 3461 (Delivery Status Notification)

p3c05.subject: Weibo's celebrity-post collapses — Li Chen's 'we' post with Fan Bingbing (27 May 2015) and Lu Han's relationship announcement (8 Oct 2017, roughly two hours of failure) — and the push/pull fanout plus ten-minute hybrid-cloud burst platform (DCP, with Alibaba Cloud) built because a single tap by one account is an unbudgetable write
people: Wang Guansheng (王关胜), Weibo platform architecture
Li Chen / Fan Bingbing (the 27 May 2015 post)
p3c05.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is that push-or-pull is not a preference, it is forced by a power-law follow graph, and the senior signal is where you put the threshold and why. Weibo is the extreme case with the extreme numbers: a follow graph more skewed than Twitter's, top accounts past 100 million followers, and a national audience that arrives inside one minute. It gives the reader something the US examples do not — the third axis. Weibo's answer was not only hybrid fanout (push to normal accounts, pull the celebrity outbox) but a second admission: push only to followers currently online, and let the rest pull on connect, plus a capacity plane that doubles the fleet in ten minutes because celebrity events cannot be provisioned for in advance. From that a reader can derive why the threshold is a function of online-follower count rather than follower count, and why the hybrid boundary has to be dynamic.
p3c05.struggle: Weibo's own engineers report the hybrid is expensive precisely where it matters: follower counts move constantly, so the per-account push/pull classification is itself mutable state that must be maintained and re-evaluated, and the complexity pushed them back toward read-diffusion for large parts of the feed. The threshold is not a constant you pick in an interview; it is a control loop you now own.
p3c05.consequence: Two hours of platform failure on 8 Oct 2017 for a service with hundreds of millions of DAU; the 2015 event drove what was reported as the largest hybrid-cloud deployment in China, provisioning on the order of a thousand nodes in ten minutes on Alibaba Cloud purely to absorb one person's post.
leads: Weibo platform engineering writeup, '微博混合云DCP：极端流量下的峰值应对与架构挑战' (Aliyun developer community; also ArchSummit/QCon Beijing, 2016-2017)
'新浪微博如何应对极端峰值下的弹性扩容挑战' — Weibo DCP elastic-scaling talk transcript, 2017
Weibo tech-team feed architecture series on 推拉结合 (push/pull hybrid) and 在线推、离线拉 (push-to-online, pull-on-connect)
Contemporary reporting on the 8 Oct 2017 Lu Han outage and the 27 May 2015 Li Chen post

p3c06.subject: Robert Torrens' Real Property Act 1858 in South Australia replaces deeds conveyancing — where two buyers could each search the chain of title, each find the seller apparently entitled, and each pay — with a single authoritative register in which the entry, not the contract, is what transfers the land
p3c06.org: Colony of South Australia, Lands Titles Office (and every Torrens jurisdiction after it)
p3c06.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is a geospatial index plus a matching lock, and Torrens supplies both halves with no software in the frame. The lock half: deeds conveyancing is read-then-act at civilisation scale — the search and the claim were separate acts by separate parties, both buyers were individually correct, and the loser's only remedy was litigation. Torrens' fix is exactly what the chapter teaches: exactly one authoritative place per resource, and the claim *is* the write at that place, not a decision reached in the claimant's head. The index half: you cannot register a parcel until the colony agrees how a parcel is named, so the Act forced a survey-plan identifier into existence first — the resource must have a canonical spatial identity before it can be claimed, which is why an Uber match needs a cell id before it needs a lock. And the residual is measurable: the gap between search and registration is still open, which is why US practice, which never adopted the register, sells insurance against exactly that window — proof that re-querying just before you act narrows the gap and does not close it.
p3c06.struggle: Making the register authoritative means the register can be wrong and you cannot roll it back. Indefeasibility protects a fraudster's innocent transferee against the true owner, so the colony had to bolt on an assurance fund — money, not a rollback, exactly the compensation the chapter's sibling ticketing problem also ends at. And a registered claim has no TTL: a caveat lodged and never resolved freezes a title indefinitely, which is the deadlock any lock without an expiry produces.
p3c06.consequence: Adopted across Australia and New Zealand within two decades, then Canada, Ireland, Singapore, Malaysia and England (Land Registry; LRA 1925, then 2002). The jurisdictions that did not adopt it — most of the United States — pay for the missing authoritative register every year: title search and title insurance are a multi-billion-dollar annual premium industry whose central product, the gap endorsement, exists solely to cover the interval between the search and the recording.
leads: Real Property Act 1858 (South Australia), 21 Vict. No. 15 — the statute itself
R. R. Torrens, 'The South Australian System of Conveyancing by Registration of Title' (Adelaide, 1859)
Frazer v Walker [1967] 1 AC 569 (Privy Council) — indefeasibility, and the assurance fund as the boundary where the register cannot be undone
ALTA Owner's Policy forms and the 'gap' endorsement; NAIC title insurance premium data — the US price of not having the register

Report of the Court of Inquiry, Board of Trade, into the Great Eastern Railway collision at Thorpe, 12 September 1874 (Railways Archive docID 111) — the demoted alternate, same race with a telegraph instead of a register

p3c07.subject: Lotus Notes replication (Iris Associates, shipped 7 December 1989): the first mass-deployed offline-first multi-master store, where two people editing the same document in different replicas produced a 'Replication or Save Conflict' document — Notes refused to merge, kept both, and handed the decision to a human
p3c07.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is that there is no algorithm that merges two arbitrary binary edits correctly, so the design goal is to detect concurrency reliably, refuse to guess, and preserve both versions where the human can see them. Notes is where that policy was invented and then load-tested by tens of millions of enterprise users for thirty years, over modems, with replicas that could be days apart. It gives the reader the mechanism's full shape: a per-document sequence/version so a save can be recognised as based on a stale base, a deterministic rule for which surviving copy is the parent, and a conflict artifact placed in the user's view rather than in a log. Delete it and 'make a conflicted copy' reads as a Dropbox quirk; with it, the reader can derive why the check has to be a compare-and-swap at the linearisation point, why last-write-wins is a data-loss machine, and why the fork must be visible in the same namespace as the file.
p3c07.struggle: Preserving both copies only works if the human looks. Notes conflict documents accumulated silently in databases for years — invisible in most views, resolved by nobody, and periodically discovered by administrators as thousands of orphaned responses. Later field-level merge helped when two people touched different fields and did nothing when they touched the same one. The mechanism converts data loss into a human backlog and then discovers the human is not processing the backlog.
p3c07.consequence: IBM took Lotus in 1995 for about $3.5B, largely for Notes; the platform ran the messaging and workflow of most of the Fortune 500 through the 1990s, and IBM sold the Notes/Domino business to HCL for $1.8B in 2018 — a full arc, with 'Replication or Save Conflict' surviving intact through all of it.
leads: Lotus Notes Release 1, 7 December 1989, Iris Associates — release documentation and design notes on replication
IBM Notes/Domino administration documentation and Redbooks on replication and save conflicts (conflict parent/response document structure, merge-replication-conflicts flag)
Ray Ozzie, Computer History Museum oral history, and his writings on Notes replication design
IBM-Lotus acquisition filings, July 1995; HCL-IBM Notes/Domino sale announcement, December 2018

p3c08.subject: IRCTC Tatkal: Indian Railways' last-minute quota opening at a fixed 10:00 clock edge, where hundreds of thousands of concurrent users contend for the same berths, the seat is blocked while the payment gateway is called, and the block expires mid-payment — money debited, no ticket, refund in a week
p3c08.org: IRCTC / CRIS (Centre for Railway Information Systems), Indian Railways
people: Indian Railways Ministry (Tatkal timing and Aadhaar-OTP rule changes)
p3c08.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is not the atomic seat claim — every candidate finds that — it is the ugly edge the claim creates: what happens when a hold expires while its owner's payment is in flight. IRCTC is that edge at national scale, every single morning, with a third-party bank gateway on the far side that has its own timeout, its own retry, and no shared transaction. It is also the only place a reader can watch the full mechanism set deployed under a regulator: the hold with an expiry, the payment-status reconciliation job that has to decide after the fact whether the debit and the booking agree, the compensating refund because you cannot roll back a bank, and the on-sale split (AC at 10:00, non-AC at 11:00) as deliberate load shedding by cutting the contention window in half. From that the reader derives why the hold TTL must exceed the worst-case gateway latency, why the reconciler is not optional, and why the honest answer to 'the hold expired and the payment succeeded' is a compensation, not a rollback.
p3c08.struggle: You cannot make the TTL long enough. Lengthen it and inventory sits locked while touts hold seats they will not buy; shorten it and honest buyers are charged for tickets they do not get. Indian Railways ended up fighting the problem outside the software entirely — splitting the on-sale times, then in July 2025 requiring Aadhaar OTP authentication for Tatkal — because the contention was never really about locking, it was about who was allowed to contend.
p3c08.consequence: Capacity was rebuilt around the burst rather than the mean: concurrent connections raised from 40,000 to 120,000 and then to 300,000, and booking throughput to roughly 15,000 tickets/minute by 2015 (later rebuilt again toward 150,000/minute), all sized for two minutes a day; meanwhile 'money debited, ticket not booked' became common enough that IRCTC publishes a standing advisory and a refund timetable for it, and bot operators exploiting the same window were prosecuted by the CBI.
leads: IRCTC advisory, 'Money debited but ticket not booked' (contents.irctc.co.in) — the operator's own statement of the failure mode and refund timeline
Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha answers and CRIS statements on PRS/e-ticketing capacity, 2014-2016 (concurrent users 40k → 120k → 300k; 15,000 tickets/min)
Ministry of Railways circulars on Tatkal timings (AC 10:00 / non-AC 11:00 split, 2015) and the Aadhaar-OTP Tatkal requirement effective 1 July 2025
CBI prosecutions of Tatkal booking software operators (2016 onward)

p3c09.subject: 1994: runaway early crawlers knock over servers on the young web, and Martijn Koster gets the www-talk list to agree on robots.txt — a plain text file, obeyed voluntarily, enforced by nothing
p3c09.org: Nexor / the www-talk mailing list (WWW Robots list)
p3c09.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is that per-host politeness and 11k fetches/sec must live in the same data structure. This story shows politeness was never a courtesy feature — it is a promise made to strangers with zero enforcement on the other side, so the only place it can be implemented is inside the crawler's own frontier, as host-keyed back-queues with a delay each. Delete it and 'be polite' reads as etiquette rather than the constraint that dictates the frontier's shape.
p3c09.struggle: The standard they landed on cannot express a rate for a specific bot, cannot authenticate a requester, and binds nobody; it took 28 years to become RFC 9309, and even then only as advisory. Koster's own writing admits the file protects the server operator only from robots that choose to read it.
p3c09.consequence: A file with no legal force became the de facto governance of the entire crawl economy — search, archiving, and now AI training scrapers — and its unenforceability is exactly what the 2024–25 AI-crawler fights are about.
leads: Martijn Koster, 'A Standard for Robot Exclusion' (June 1994, robotstxt.org)
www-talk@www0.cern.ch archive, Feb–Jun 1994 threads on robot exclusion (first mention 25 Feb 1994)
RFC 9309, Robots Exclusion Protocol (September 2022)
Charles Stross's published account of the Websnarf crawler that hammered Koster's server, emails dated 7 March 1994

p3c10.subject: 11 March 2011: in the minutes after the Tōhoku earthquake, NTT DoCoMo restricts 80% of voice call attempts across Tōhoku and Kantō (90% in places) while leaving packet traffic largely open
p3c10.org: NTT DoCoMo / Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC)
p3c10.why_kernel: The crux is that the counter is shared state and no one can consult it per request. A national carrier facing 60× normal call volume did not build a global counter; it computed one number centrally and pushed a drop percentage to every switch, enforced locally, with no coordination per call. That is the 'accept N× error with local counters' branch of the kernel executed at country scale — and it makes the trade concrete: the limiter stayed up and correct-ish, the accounting was wrong everywhere, and that was the right call.
p3c10.struggle: A percentage drop is blind. It rejected safety-confirmation calls at the same rate as everything else, and DoCoMo had no way to make the throttle scope-aware in the moment; the actual remedy was a different product (the disaster message board, and packet-first policy) rather than a smarter counter.
p3c10.consequence: Voice connect rates fell to a few percent for days across the affected regions while millions tried to reach family; the failure drove MIC's post-disaster study group and a formal policy shift toward prioritising packet and message-board capacity over voice in emergencies.
leads: NTT DoCoMo press release, 30 March 2011: 'Damage and Restoration Status Regarding the Tohoku-Pacific Ocean Earthquake' (states 80%/90% voice restriction, 30% packet in Miyagi)
MIC, 'Intermediate Report on Maintaining Communications Capabilities during Major Disasters', 21 September 2011
NTT DOCOMO Technical Journal, disaster-response network control articles, 2011–2012
ITU-T Q.1248 automatic call gapping — the standing mechanism the restriction was applied through

p3c11.subject: June 2012: a botched CA-7 batch-scheduler upgrade at RBS/NatWest/Ulster Bank destroys the overnight job queue; 6.5 million customers lose access to their money for days, Ulster Bank for nearly a month
p3c11.org: Royal Bank of Scotland / NatWest / Ulster Bank (CA-7 scheduler)
p3c11.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is that a due job must fire exactly once and that misfire policy is a real design decision. RBS shows the zero-firings half with the arithmetic attached: the scheduler's queue is durable state that cannot be recomputed, and a missed night does not delay work, it compounds it against the next night's window, which is already full. That derives durable due-state, ordered dependency, catch-up policy, and why 'we'll just rerun it' is not available.
p3c11.struggle: There was no safe replay. Re-running the batch out of order produced wrong balances and interest, so recovery was partly manual and ran for weeks; the backlog grew faster than they could clear it because each night added a fresh batch on top.
p3c11.consequence: £56M in regulatory fines (FCA £42M + PRA £14M, November 2014), roughly £175M in customer redress and remediation, 6.5M customers, missed mortgage payments, payroll failures, and people stranded abroad.
leads: FCA Final Notice to Royal Bank of Scotland plc, National Westminster Bank plc and Ulster Bank Ltd, 19 November 2014
PRA Final Notice, November 2014 (£14M)
FCA press release, 'FCA fines RBS, NatWest and Ulster Bank Ltd £42 million for IT failures'
UK Treasury Select Committee correspondence with RBS on the June 2012 IT incident (2012)

p3c12.subject: 2002–2005: AT&T Labs has to find the heavy hitters on OC-48 backbone links where per-flow counters cannot fit in memory — Gigascope in production, and Cormode & Muthukrishnan's Count-Min sketch, deliberately wrong in one direction only
p3c12.why_kernel: The chapter's move is 'be wrong on purpose, in a direction you control, and name who it hurts.' This is where that guarantee was engineered rather than assumed: with a fixed memory budget on a 500GB/day stream, the design choice is the sign of your error, and Count-Min's never-underestimate property is precisely what makes a top-K list safe to act on. Without it, 'use a sketch' is a vocabulary word; with it, a reader can derive why the fast path is approximate, why the error is one-sided, and why an exact batch path must exist behind it.
p3c12.struggle: Sketch error is proportional to total stream volume, so a spam flood raises the noise floor for every key you are trying to measure — the attack degrades the detector. And a sketch answers counts, not keys: you still need a separate candidate structure to know which items to interrogate, which is the whole reason heavy-hitter algorithms and sketches are two different things.
p3c12.consequence: Became the real-time detection layer for worm and DDoS events on a tier-1 backbone (Slammer-era, ten billion records a day), and Count-Min is now the default counting structure inside effectively every trending, telemetry and analytics stack shipped since.
leads: Cranor, Johnson, Spatscheck, Shkapenyuk, 'Gigascope: A Stream Database for Network Applications', SIGMOD 2003

Metwally, Agrawal, El Abbadi, 'Efficient Computation of Frequent and Top-k Elements in Data Streams', ICDT 2005 (Space-Saving)

p3c13.subject: August–September 2021: the Media Rating Council suspends accreditation of Nielsen's national and local TV ratings after a pandemic-era undercount of roughly 2–6% — the numbers that price tens of billions of dollars of US advertising
p3c13.why_kernel: The chapter turns on 'the count is a line item on an invoice, and auditability is a requirement, not paranoia.' This is what happens when the billing counter cannot be audited: because Nielsen's number is a modelled panel estimate rather than a retained event log, the dispute could not be settled by recount — only by re-modelling and argument. That derives, negatively, every property the chapter demands of the exact path: raw events retained, deduplicated deterministically, recomputable on demand by an outsider.
p3c13.struggle: There is no recount. Once the measurement is a sample plus a model, an outside auditor can only say the model is wrong, never say what the right number was — so the industry's remedy was to shop for a different vendor rather than fix the figure.
p3c13.consequence: The suspension triggered make-good demands, accelerated the 'alternative currencies' push, and preceded Nielsen's $16B take-private in 2022; accreditation was not restored until 2023. (The often-quoted per-point dollar extrapolation is an inference, not a reported figure — hedge or drop it.)
leads: MRC public statement suspending accreditation of Nielsen national and local TV services, 30 August–1 September 2021
VAB letter to the MRC alleging systematic undercount, April 2021
Nielsen client letter acknowledging 'understatement of audience estimates', May 2021
MRC audit and reinstatement decision documents, 2023

p3c14.subject: 20–21 November 1985: a counter overflow in Bank of New York's government-securities software leaves it unable to record deliveries; securities keep arriving all day and it borrows roughly $23 billion overnight from the Fed's discount window to cover the gap
p3c14.org: Bank of New York / Federal Reserve Bank of New York
p3c14.why_kernel: The chapter's crux is idempotency and the ledger. This is the ledger half at maximum voltage: the record is not bookkeeping downstream of the money, it is the gate — and when the write fails, the transfers do not stop arriving. The gap between 'effect happened' and 'effect recorded' was denominated in billions inside a single business day. From that a reader derives why the record must be written in the same transaction as the effect, why the ledger is append-only, and why reconciliation against the counterparty is a first-class subsystem rather than a nightly chore.
p3c14.struggle: They could not stop the inbound flow — Fedwire deliveries are one-directional and counterparties kept sending — and they could not reconstruct the day's positions from what they had. The Fed lent against essentially the bank's whole loan portfolio as collateral because nobody could say what the bank owned.
p3c14.consequence: ~$23B overnight advance, the largest discount-window loan in Fed history; roughly $5M in interest paid on one night; House Banking Committee hearings; and it pushed the government-securities market toward a central clearing corporation and Fedwire safeguards.
leads: McAndrews & Potter, 'The Liquidity Effects of the Events of September 11, 2001', FRBNY Economic Policy Review, 2002 (recounts the 1985 BoNY episode)
Richmond Fed Working Paper 03-16 (2003), payment system disruptions and the Federal Reserve
US House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs hearings on the Bank of New York computer failure, 1985–86
Juncker, Summers & Young, 'A Primer on the Settlement of Payments in the United States', Federal Reserve Bulletin 1991

p3c15.subject: Google Wave: Google's own attempt to run operational transformation between independent federated servers — launched at I/O in May 2009, opened to the public that September, killed on 4 August 2010 — and the concurrency-control design it published on the way out, in which every wavelet still has exactly one hosting server that serialises operations, because federation could not remove the sequencer
p3c15.why_kernel: The chapter must justify committing to OT behind a single sequencer rather than saying 'both branches are valid'. Wave is the controlled experiment, run by the same company in the same years: Google set out to make collaborative editing federate across servers it did not own, published the protocol, and the published concurrency-control design still routes every operation through one hosting server per wavelet — because the peer-to-peer transform property is exactly where OT breaks (which p2c04 has already shown the reader by counterexample). Then Wave died and Docs, same company, shipped the same algorithm with the sequencer as an uncontroversial assumption. From that the reader derives that the server is not an infrastructure convenience but the correctness condition; that what CRDTs buy is the deletion of that server; and what they pay for it is per-character identity that never shrinks.
p3c15.struggle: Federation was the entire pitch and the part that never worked: operations still had to reach the wavelet's host, so a 'federated' wave was only as available as one server, and the open-source successor reached the Apache Attic in January 2018 with no production federation ever running. And the correctness story was the easy half — Wave shipped before anyone could explain to a user what a wave was.
p3c15.consequence: A flagship launch shut down inside fifteen months and donated to Apache; real-time collaborative editing moved into Google Docs (April 2010) where the central sequencer is unremarkable. Every mainstream editor since — Docs, Office 365, Figma, Notion — pins a sequencer, and the federated branch became the CRDT research programme instead of a product.
leads: David Wang, Alex Mah, Soren Lassen, 'Google Wave Operational Transformation' whitepaper, Google, July 2010
Google Wave Federation Protocol specification and the Wave Protocol open-source release, 2009–2010
Urs Hölzle, 'Update on Google Wave', Google Official Blog, 4 August 2010
Apache Wave move to the Attic, January 2018 — the end of the federated branch

p3c16.subject: May 2003: LiveJournal's databases are melting on donated hardware, there is no money for more, and Brad Fitzpatrick writes memcached in Perl in a few days — using the spare RAM already sitting in the web servers, with cache servers that never speak to each other
p3c16.why_kernel: The chapter's thesis is 'a cache is the one distributed system allowed to forget — now design like you mean it.' Memcached is that sentence compiled: no replication, no persistence, no server-to-server membership, hashing done in the client, eviction as a normal event. Every one of those deletions is purchased with the forgetting property, under a budget of literally zero dollars. Without the story the dumb-server/smart-client shape looks like an arbitrary architecture; with it the reader can re-derive each omission from what a miss costs.
p3c16.struggle: With no membership protocol, adding a node reshuffles the keyspace and the resulting miss storm lands on the database that was already the emergency — the exact hole that consistent hashing, then leases and gutter pools, were later bolted on to patch. The design's cheapness and its stampede problem are the same decision.
p3c16.consequence: LiveJournal survived on a few dozen machines instead of a hardware budget it did not have, and memcached became the default cache of the 2000s web — carrying its defaults, slab allocator and absent auth included, into Facebook, Wikipedia, YouTube and Twitter.
leads: Brad Fitzpatrick, 'Distributed Caching with Memcached', Linux Journal #124, August 2004
Fitzpatrick, 'LiveJournal's Backend: A History of Scaling' slide deck, USENIX/OSCON 2004 (danga.com)
The original May 2003 Perl prototype of memcached, published by Fitzpatrick
memcached release history and protocol.txt in the danga/memcached repository

p3c17.subject: Mendel Rosenblum and John Ousterhout build the Log-Structured File System in the Sprite OS at Berkeley — the disk's only on-disk structure is an append-only log — and then Margo Seltzer's benchmarks show the segment cleaner eating the win
p3c17.org: UC Berkeley (Sprite project) / Harvard, later BSD-LFS
p3c17.why_kernel: It is the first system built on the premise the chapter teaches — that the log is not a recovery aid bolted onto real storage but the storage itself — and it measures the two numbers that make Kafka's whole shape inevitable (sequential writes reach ~70% of disk bandwidth against 5-10% for update-in-place), from which a reader can derive segment files, offsets as byte positions, page-cache reads, and above all that retention and compaction are not features but the tax a log charges for being the truth.
p3c17.struggle: The cleaner. Reclaiming space from a log means rewriting live data, and under random-update transaction workloads Seltzer measured LFS losing to the file system it was supposed to replace; Ousterhout published a public critique of her measurements, she published a response, and the argument was never settled — Sprite died, BSD-LFS was shipped and then left to rot, and the log-as-truth idea won everywhere except the workstation it was designed for.
p3c17.consequence: No dollar figure — the cost was the design losing the war it was built for. What it set off is the entire lineage the chapter stands on: NetApp's WAFL, flash translation layers, LSM trees (Bigtable, LevelDB, RocksDB), and Kafka's segment-plus-compaction storage layer, which is LFS's cleaner with a retention policy stapled to it.
leads: Rosenblum & Ousterhout, 'The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System', SOSP '91 / ACM TOCS 10(1), Feb 1992
Seltzer, Smith, Balakrishnan, Chang, McMains, Padmanabhan, 'File System Logging Versus Clustering: A Performance Comparison', USENIX Winter 1995
Ousterhout, 'A Critique of Seltzer's LFS Measurements' (1995) and Seltzer et al., 'A Response to Ousterhout's Critique of LFS Measurements'

p3c18.subject: 14 August 2003: the alarm processor in FirstEnergy's Akron control room dies of a race condition in GE Energy's XA/21 EMS, fails silently, takes both the primary and the backup EMS server with it, and leaves operators watching an hour-stale grid while 61,800 MW cascades off across eight states and Ontario
p3c18.org: FirstEnergy / GE Energy (XA/21) / NERC / U.S.-Canada Power System Outage Task Force
people: Kevin Poulsen (reporter who obtained GE's account)
p3c18.why_kernel: It is the real version of the chapter's invented cold open, and it derives the non-functional requirement the chapter says interviewers listen for: the monitoring plane must sit outside the blast radius of what it watches, and it must alert on its own staleness, because a monitor that has silently stopped is pixel-identical to a monitor showing a healthy system — the operators were not misinformed, they were confidently uninformed. Honest caveat: it derives the self-dependency and meta-monitoring half of this chapter, not the cardinality half.
p3c18.struggle: They never got the alarms back. The wall is epistemic, not technical: with the EMS silent there was no signal distinguishable from calm, so the only remaining monitoring was neighbouring utilities telephoning to ask what was happening, and by the time anyone believed the grid was in trouble the cascade took seven minutes. GE found the bug only in a post-hoc code audit and shipped a quiet patch months later.
p3c18.consequence: ~50 million people dark, 61,800 MW lost, 11 deaths, $4-10 billion in US economic losses plus a 0.7% drop in Ontario's monthly GDP. Downstream: the Energy Policy Act of 2005 made NERC reliability standards mandatory and fineable, converting 'we monitor our grid' from a promise into an audited obligation.
leads: U.S.-Canada Power System Outage Task Force, 'Final Report on the August 14, 2003 Blackout in the United States and Canada: Causes and Recommendations', April 2004 (Ch. 5, the alarm and EMS failures)
Kevin Poulsen, 'Software Bug Contributed to Blackout', SecurityFocus, 11 February 2004 (GE Energy's own account of the race condition)
Energy Policy Act of 2005, §1211 — mandatory reliability standards, the regulatory consequence
Tobias Oetiker, MRTG (1994) and RRDtool (1999) documentation — the demoted alternate, and the source for the cardinality half this story does not cover

p3c19.subject: Father Roberto Busa talks Thomas J. Watson Sr. into lending IBM's punched-card machines to build a complete concordance of Thomas Aquinas — 11 million words of medieval Latin turned into a term-to-location index, one card per word, over thirty years
p3c19.org: Pontifical Gregorian University / CAAL, Gallarate, Italy (machines and staffing from IBM)
p3c19.why_kernel: Strip the computers away and the inverted index is still there: the reader watches the map from term to posting list get physically manufactured, and derives from the manufacture itself the three structural costs the chapter spends its budget on — the index is a separate artifact built offline from the documents, the analyzer (here, Latin lemmatisation: amabat to amare) decides what a term even is, and the dominant cost is sorting and merging postings, not looking them up. Nothing in the chapter otherwise explains why an index has to be built rather than queried.
p3c19.struggle: The sorter could order cards on one field at a time, so every analysis decision had to be materialised as another pass over 11 million cards, and lemmatising Latin could not be mechanised at all — a human had to decide which lemma each form belonged to. That human step, not the machines, consumed the three decades. Busa was in his seventies when the printed index was finished.
p3c19.consequence: IBM carried the machine time and staffing for roughly thirty years; the output was 56 folio volumes published 1974-1980, then a CD-ROM in 1992. Downstream it founded concordancing and digital humanities, and fixed the concordance's data structure — term, then the sorted list of where it occurs — as the shape every later text search engine inherited.
leads: Roberto Busa, 'The Annals of Humanities Computing: The Index Thomisticus', Computers and the Humanities 14(2), 1980, pp. 83-90
Index Thomisticus (Frommann-Holzboog, 56 vols., 1974-1980), editorial front matter on method
Steven E. Jones, 'Roberto Busa, S.J., and the Emergence of Humanities Computing' (Routledge, 2016), which works from IBM archival records of the 1949 Watson meeting

p3c20.subject: Microsoft replaces 3x replication in Windows Azure Storage with Local Reconstruction Codes, dropping overhead to 1.33x — and picks the code not for its storage cost but for how few fragments a repair has to read
p3c20.why_kernel: This is the only public account where repair cost, not redundancy ratio, chooses the code — the team rejected plain Reed-Solomon because every lost fragment costs k reads across the network, and at cloud failure rates that repair traffic both saturates the fabric and lengthens the window in which a second loss kills you. From it a reader derives the chapter's least obvious claim, that repair speed is a durability input rather than an operations detail, plus why the hot write path keeps 3x replication and only sealed, immutable extents get erasure-coded.
p3c20.struggle: LRC buys cheap repair by adding local parity groups, which costs 0.33x back, and it is not maximum-distance-separable: some four-fragment loss patterns are simply undecodable. They had to computer-search coefficients over a small finite field and then prove 'maximal recoverability' to bound which patterns they were choosing to lose. The write path never got the savings at all — you cannot erasure-code data that is still being appended to.
p3c20.consequence: 3x to 1.33x across an exabyte-class fleet — hundreds of millions of dollars of drives not bought — plus USENIX ATC 2012 Best Paper and adoption across every Microsoft storage line from cloud to desktop. And a permanent architectural split in the product between hot 3x storage and sealed coded storage.
leads: Huang, Simitci, Xu, Ogus, Calder, Gopalan, Li, Yekhanin, 'Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage', USENIX ATC 2012 (Best Paper)
Calder et al., 'Windows Azure Storage: A Highly Available Cloud Storage Service with Strong Consistency', SOSP 2011 — extents, sealing, and the 3x hot path
Gopalan, Huang, Simitci, Yekhanin, 'On the Locality of Codeword Symbols', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2012 — the maximal-recoverability bound

p3c21.subject: Move Networks, a Utah company founded by NetWare architect Drew Major, ships adaptive bitrate streaming for ABC's and Fox's full-episode players — chopping every video into short chunks encoded at several bitrates, served as ordinary cacheable HTTP GETs, with the client choosing the rung
p3c21.org: Move Networks (American Fork, Utah), for ABC / Fox / ESPN / Comcast Fancast
people: Roger Pantos (Apple, who later standardised the idea as HLS)
p3c21.why_kernel: Both halves of this chapter's crux fall out of this one decision. Because the client picks a rung per chunk, the encoder must produce the whole ladder up front — that is the transcoding DAG's reason to exist — and because a chunk is a plain immutable HTTP object, delivery becomes a cache-hit-rate and peering problem rather than a stateful streaming-server problem, which is the entire CDN-economics conversation. Without this the ladder reads as an arbitrary product choice instead of a forced consequence of one 3 Mbps phone in Jakarta. Scope the claim precisely: multi-bitrate switching already existed inside stateful protocols (RealNetworks SureStream 1998, Microsoft Intelligent Streaming 1999) — what Move did first at network scale was chunked, cacheable, client-driven HTTP.
p3c21.struggle: The mechanism was right and the packaging was fatal: Move needed a proprietary browser plugin and its own server, so when Apple published the same idea in 2009 as a text playlist over plain HTTP with nothing to install, the standard erased the company that invented it. The ladder they bequeathed also locked the industry into encoding everything up front for viewers who mostly never arrive — the exact cost problem the chapter's UGC pipeline has to solve.
p3c21.consequence: Within three years Smooth Streaming, HLS, HDS, MPEG-DASH and Netflix all shipped the same architecture. Move raised over $60M, was sold to EchoStar for roughly $45M in 2011, and its patents ended their life as ammunition in Dish's streaming litigation.
leads: US Patent 7,818,444 B2, 'Apparatus, system, and method for multi-bitrate content streaming' (Major et al., Move Networks, granted October 2010) — and its continuation US 8,868,772
RFC 8216, 'HTTP Live Streaming' (Pantos & May, August 2017); the original draft-pantos-http-live-streaming-00, May 2009
EchoStar Corporation press release and SEC filings, January 2011, on the acquisition of Move Networks' assets
RealNetworks SureStream (RealSystem G2, 1998) and Microsoft Intelligent Streaming (1999) — the prior art the claim must be scoped against

p3c22.subject: 1 October 2020: a memory fault in one of arrowhead's shared NAS devices fails to trigger automatic failover because of a single miswritten switchover setting, and the Tokyo Stock Exchange halts all 3,700 listed names for the entire day rather than reboot
p3c22.org: Tokyo Stock Exchange / Japan Exchange Group / Fujitsu
p3c22.why_kernel: The revealing fact is not the hardware fault, it is why they refused to restart: a reboot would have silently discarded orders that member firms still believed were live, and no rule existed for what 'your order is gone' means. That derives the chapter's crux directly — in an exchange the product is the single authoritative ordered sequence of events, so recovery cannot mean 'bring the service back up', it must mean 'reconstruct the identical sequence', which is exactly why the hot path is one deterministic thread fed from a journal and why an opaque failover is worse than a halt.
p3c22.struggle: They could have restarted by mid-morning and chose not to, because price-time priority is only meaningful if every participant agrees on the same arrival order, and after the storage failure nobody could reconstruct that agreement. The wall was a governance gap, not a code path: the sequence was recoverable in principle and unrecoverable in practice because the market had never defined the procedure.
p3c22.consequence: A full trading day of a roughly $6 trillion market lost — the first all-day halt since TSE went fully electronic in 1999. President Koichiro Miyahara resigned in November 2020, the FSA issued a business improvement order, and TSE spent six months writing the mid-session reboot rulebook it had never had, in force from April 2021.
leads: Japan Exchange Group, 'The Failure of Equity Trading System on October 1, 2020', 19 October 2020, plus the independent investigation committee report, November 2020
JPX, 'Trading resumption through a system reboot' — public consultation January 2021, rules effective April 2021
Financial Services Agency business improvement order to TSE and JPX, 27 November 2020

p3c23.subject: Orca, from Seoul National University and FriendliAI, replaces request-level batching with iteration-level scheduling plus selective batching — the mechanism the industry now calls continuous batching — a year before any open-source stack had it
p3c23.why_kernel: It isolates the throughput half of the chapter's crux and shows the reasoning that produces it: generation lengths differ wildly, so a batch scheduled per request makes every short answer wait on the longest one and leaves the GPU idle for most of the batch's life; scheduling per decoding iteration instead lets finished requests leave and new ones join mid-flight. From that a reader can derive why 'batch size' in LLM serving is not a tuning knob but a question about how much KV cache is resident right now — which is the sentence the chapter's later PagedAttention story assumes you already accept.
p3c23.struggle: Fixing the scheduler exposed the allocator. Orca still reserved contiguous KV cache sized to each request's maximum possible length, so memory fragmentation, not compute, capped how many requests could actually be in flight — the win was real and immediately bounded by the next wall. And the system was never open-sourced; the idea sat inside a company for a year while everyone else served requests one batch at a time.
p3c23.consequence: 36.9x throughput over NVIDIA FasterTransformer at equal latency on GPT-3 175B. Continuous batching is now the default in vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and every commercial endpoint, which means most of the industry's serving cost per token was set by a scheduling decision published at OSDI and ignored for twelve months.
leads: Yu, Jeong, Kim, Kim, Chun, 'Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models', OSDI 2022
USENIX OSDI '22 recorded conference talk and slides for the same paper
NVIDIA FasterTransformer (v4/v5) source as the request-level-batching baseline Orca measures against

p3c24.subject: Roger Weber, Hans-Jorg Schek and Stephen Blott at ETH Zurich prove that above roughly ten dimensions every tree index for similarity search loses to a plain sequential scan, then propose the VA-File — an admission that the scan is unavoidable and can only be made cheaper
p3c24.org: ETH Zurich (Institute of Information Systems) / Bell Labs
people: Kevin Beyer and Raghu Ramakrishnan (the ICDT'99 companion result)
p3c24.why_kernel: This is the result that makes approximation compulsory rather than pragmatic. A reader who has it can derive why the recall-latency-memory triangle exists at all — geometry, not engineering laziness — and can therefore state the only sane question about a billion-vector index ('what recall, at what latency, at what memory cost') instead of asking which index is correct. Without it, HNSW and IVF look like clever optimisations of a solvable problem, and the chapter's whole framing of approximation as a negotiated tradeoff has no floor under it.
p3c24.struggle: Their own fix barely helps. The VA-File makes the unavoidable scan cheaper by a constant factor and nothing more; the paper's honest conclusion is that no index beats scanning asymptotically in high dimensions, so anything genuinely faster must stop being exact. They set out to build a better index and published a proof that better indexes do not exist.
p3c24.consequence: It effectively ended a decade of multidimensional-index research — R*-tree, X-tree, SS-tree, SR-tree — and redirected the field to approximation, with LSH arriving the same year and graph and quantization indexes following. It also fixed brute-force scan as the honest baseline that every ANN benchmark, including the ones behind today's vector databases, still has to report against.
leads: Weber, Schek, Blott, 'A Quantitative Analysis and Performance Study for Similarity-Search Methods in High-Dimensional Spaces', VLDB 1998, pp. 194-205
Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan, Shaft, 'When Is "Nearest Neighbor" Meaningful?', ICDT 1999
Indyk & Motwani, 'Approximate Nearest Neighbors: Towards Removing the Curse of Dimensionality', STOC 1998
